# ASD STIG: what your app inherits from the IdP, and what it still owns

This is the default split for an application that delegates **all** sign-in to the hardened Keycloak (authorization code + PKCE through this skill's integration). It does not depend on your app, so you can plan with it now. For your ATO package, ask the IdP operator for two things: the IdP's own checklist (`.ckl`/`.cklb` from `kcstig.py verify`) as the inherited evidence, and the inheritance statement for your client (`kcstig.py inherit --profile <idp profile> --app <client_id>`). That statement is authoritative for the operator's realm and has the same three groups as the tables below.

Rules for writing this up (an assessor will check them):

- Cite rules individually, never as ranges. A range silently includes rules the IdP does not satisfy.
- Take IDs and CAT levels from this file or the operator's tool output, not from memory.
- An inherited rule is inherited only while every sign-in goes through the IdP. A local login form, API key or back door in the app puts the rule back on the app.

| Group | Rules | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Inherited from the IdP | 86 | Mark inherited; attach the IdP checklist as evidence |
| Shared | 53 | The IdP does its part; the app must do the rest (see the table) |
| Application | 47 | The app's own code and design |
| Platform / process / conditional | 100 | Hosting, procedures, or N/A conditions: neither the IdP nor app code (NA-COND 11, PLATFORM 48, PROCESS 41) |

## Shared: what the app must still do

These are where integrations fail assessments. The integration guide (`integration.md`) implements the session, logoff, cookie, role, last-logon and logout-connection rows. A few rows name an IdP-operator or ISSO action instead (unlock procedure, Alt Tokens, CRL refresh, PIV/FICAM scope, audit-log access): those are the operator's, and the app's checklist points at the IdP's evidence for them. Rows with no specific action apply the requirement to the app's own sessions, logs, errors and connections.
